comparisons.title: Published no-alarm fractions vs Model C 2.0 V fractions
comparisons.statement: The published no-alarm statements and Model C's 2.0 V fractions must not be combined: the 2018 and 2021 documents describe ISS-detector alarm behaviour in the SAME tests without denominators, while Model C counts SAME plus SAME-R primary runs whose measured scatter reached a derived 2.0 V level.
comparisons.detail: Side by side, Kapton stayed below 2.0 V in 12 of 21 primary runs and Teflon in 11 of 15, but the definitions (alarm behaviour vs a threshold label), test sets (SAME vs SAME + SAME-R) and denominators differ, so neither result confirms or refutes the other numerically.

definition: detector would not have alarmed (Figure 9 threshold lines)
test_set: SAME flight tests analysed in 2018 (no denominators)
SAME + SAME-R primary heating runs (21 Kapton, 15 Teflon)

comparisons.title: 2018 'over half' vs 2021 'half'
comparisons.statement: The 2021 white paper's 'half' (Kapton) and 'two-thirds' (Teflon) restate the 2018 paper's 'over half' and 'about two thirds'; they are the same result, not independent confirmation.
comparisons.detail: Counting both would double-count one experiment. The 2021 wording is slightly weaker for Kapton ('half' vs 'over half').

comparisons.title: From experimental limitation to open technology need
comparisons.statement: The 2018 experiments showed that spacecraft detectors missed small-particle smokes; the 2021 white paper turned this into research questions on fuels, gravity, exploration atmospheres and multi-sensor detection; the 2025 SBIR call still lists selective, multi-property sensing as an open need and still reports frequent ISS false alarms.
comparisons.detail: 2026 follow-up work (dust-tolerant prototypes, the Saffire IV-VI time-to-alarm analysis, gas analyzers) addresses parts of these needs, but within the examined sources none closes the Kapton/Teflon or partial-gravity questions. The 2026 status is limited to the documents found and is not exhaustive.

stages.label: Experiment reports (SAME 2010, SAME-R 2014)
stages.summary: Flight data show small Kapton/Teflon particles and erratic light-scattering response; the team already calls for dust-immune detection for lunar missions and demonstrates a two-moment prototype.

stages.label: Experimental limitation (NASA/NIST)
stages.summary: Neither spacecraft detector sensed every smoke; the ISS detector would not have alarmed for over half of Kapton and about two thirds of Teflon tests.

stages.label: Research questions (decadal white paper)
stages.summary: Restates the SAME result and asks how fuels, lunar gravity and exploration atmospheres change fire signatures; proposes multi-sensor networks.

stages.label: Open technology needs (SBIR, ICES)
stages.summary: Selective, multi-property, small-particle sensing for reduced-pressure, elevated-O2 habitats; frequent ISS false alarms; no NASA smoke-detector performance standard.

stages.label: Status in reachable sources
stages.summary: Partial-gravity detector development at NASA Glenn, Saffire IV-VI time-to-alarm results at exploration-like atmospheres, deployed gas analyzers; not an exhaustive survey.

links.note: Single-property detection limitation reappears as the 2025 multi-property sensing need.
Small-particle sensitivity reappears as the 2025 small-size-range and selective-detection need.
Dust false alarms still reported in 2025; first discriminating prototypes.
Exploration-atmosphere sensing is a 2025 need; Saffire IV-VI gives flaming-fire data in 2026.
Lunar-gravity smoke transport: simulation in 2023, still a measurement gap in 2025.
Testing with real spacecraft-material smoke led to a transfer-standard need (2020); no NASA smoke-detector performance standard as of 2025.
